This varies so much by location though. I think it would be better to look at the salary search on Indeed if you're looking to start a new job.

That way you can enter negotiations with a legitimate source and print out, not a bunch of random numbers from strangers on voat.

Problem with Indeed is it is also mostly nationally based. And it does nothing to curtail the crazy/creative job titling that a lot of companies are guilty of. Discussion of what you do, and what you're paid doing it is beneficial.

So those of us moving into new positions know what it is we can potentially ask for, without over or under shooting our chances and future pay.

This discussion will in no way help with that. People aren't paid for a job title- they're paid for contributing value. Saying "This person has the same job title that I do, so we should be paid the same amount" is a fiction that has caused a lot of trouble. I've been in jobs where I knew I was making less than most of the rest of the department. In both of those cases, I also had the least experience at what I was doing. Wasn't the most pleasant feeling in the world, but I wasn't going to get the job I wanted if I started demanding the same salary of the people who had been doing it for years longer than I had.

And then there are regional issues. I make less where I live than the same job title on California or New York. Of course, my house doesn't cost 7 figures, either. But if I had asked for the annual salary of my equivalent in LA or NYC, I'd have never been hired.

If this really is just making sure you get a fair deal for yourself, then staffing firms are a great resource. They know what local companies pay for people who do what you want to do. They also get paid based on the salary the negotiate for you- thus saving you the hassle of doing it yourself. Which is great if you suck at salary negotiations. Which I do.
